IMPLEMENTATION OF AML/CFT MEASURES 
GOOD AND POOR PRACTICES 
For Money Exchange Establishments 
 
 
April 2021

2 
 
Introduction 
 
1- This guidance paper highlights the best practices implemented by some of the 
licensed Money Exchange Establishments (MEEs) in their efforts to Combating 
Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing. 
 
2- This paper reiterates the requirement of the financial institutions to remain in 
compliance with the Law on Combating Money Laundering (‘ML’) and Terrorism 
Financing (‘TF’) no. 30/2016 and supervisory instructions issued by the Central 
Bank of Oman vide ME 30. 
 
3- While the paper does not impose any new regulatory obligations, MEEs should 
nevertheless study and leverage on the guidance within to identify and address 
gaps in execution of controls with regard to Business risk assessment, Customer 
onboarding and Transaction Monitoring to more effectively mitigate its ML/TF 
risks. 
 
4- While this guidance paper is mainly derived from CBO’s off-site and on-site 
surveillance findings, the supervisory expectations and best practices therein are, 
with the appropriate modifications, equally relevant and applicable to all Money 
Exchange Establishments.  
 
5- MEEs should therefore incorporate the points from this guidance in a risk-based 
and proportionate manner, considering the outcome of national risk assessment, 
the profile of their business activities and customers. In doing so, MEEs should 
note that the takeaways in this paper are non-exhaustive, and they should 
continue to strengthen and refine their measures to manage its ML/TF risk 
efficiently and effectively. 
 
6- The Guidance consists of four chapters:  
 
a. Chapter One - Consolidated list of examples of compliant (good) and non-
compliant (poor) practices  
b. Chapter Two - Risk based approach - On-boarding customers and 
correspondents  
c. Chapter Three - Transaction Monitoring 
d. Chapter Four – Other General Guidelines 

 
 
 
3

non-compliant (poor) practices 
1.1 -  Governance, internal control, AML/CFT policies and procedures 
Examples of compliant / good practice 
Examples of non-compliance / poor practice

of

and 
Senior

ML/TF

requirements of AML/CFT legislation

procedures

more

instructions) are kept up to date and 
reviewed 
periodically 
whenever

FATF. 
 
 AML/CFT policies cover respective 
responsibilities of the staff in relation 
to overriding ML/TF risk ratings 
(residual or inherent risk) and/or client 
risk ratings; AML/CFT policies contain 
detailed provisions of the process to 
ensure consistency of the approach to

 To 
ensure

Correspondent 
Arrangements satisfy the AML/CFT 
internal 
control

and

 Board of directors and Senior Management 
demonstrates lack of commitment to ML/TF 
risk management.  
 
  AML/CFT policies and procedures are not 
comprehensive and up to date.  
 
 Senior management does not ensure that 
required resources are made available to 
manage ML/TF risks effectively e.g., human, 
technical (IT systems for monitoring) or 
financial resources.  
 
 Senior Management does not ensure that 
AML/CFT related policies and controls are 
implemented effectively; AML/CFT policies 
are not designed to tackle the ML/TF risks 
relevant to business. 
 
 AML/CFT policies lack detailed instructions 
on handling of alerts to ensure timely 
reporting to NCFI , particularly with regard to 
turn around time for reporting the case to 
NFCI after detection of the incidents/alerts.   
 
 The policies do not cover respective 
responsibilities of the staff in relation to 
overriding ML/TF risk ratings (residual or 
inherent risk) and/or client risk ratings; lack 
detailed provisions of the process to ensure 
consistency of the approach to overriding 
risk ratings and proper documentation to 
ensure changes in risk level are properly 
justified.

1.2 -  Documented ML and TF Risk Assessment 
Examples of compliant / good practice 
Examples of non-compliance / poor practice 
 The 
business 
wide 
ML/TF 
risk 
assessment (hereinafter – BRA) is 
comprehensive and identifies, at a 
minimum, ML/TF risk posed by 
customers, product and services, 
delivery channels and geographical 
exposure.  
 
 ML and TF risks in BRA are sufficiently 
differentiated. 
 
 Comprehensive 
methodology 
for 
BRAs is in place; BRA’s conclusions on 
inherent 
risks 
and 
control 
vulnerabilities are largely supported 
by quantitative data (statistics) and 
qualitative information. 
 
 The residual risk is calculated by 
taking into account inherent risk and 
controls.  
 
 Risk of new products, services and 
delivery channels are assessed  based 
on proper risk matrix and covered the 
related risk factors, before launch.  
(risk factors indicated in related  FATF 
typologies; e.g. anonymity, customer 
segment, access to cash, methods of 
funding, limits (geographic, usage, 
value)). 
 
 Risk mitigation plan is approved by 
senior management; the document 
lists detailed measures to mitigate the 
risks, implementation timelines and 
allocate 
the 
responsibilities 
for 
units/departments and employees 
involved.  
 
 
 Assessing inherent risk without properly 
analyzing all the risks associated with 
customers, 
products 
and 
services, 
geographical 
locations 
and 
delivery 
channels, and their relations to customer 
base, volume and value of transactions.  
 
 Not 
covering 
correspondent 
agent 
arrangements. 
 
 No comprehensive methodology for BRAs is 
in place. 
 
 Not assessing the variables such as the 
number of clients per product/service, number 
and value of their transactions, etc. when 
conducting 
risk 
assessment 
of 
the 
products/services.  
 
 Not assessing the direct and indirect factors 
affecting the inherent risk and controls 
which would lead to introducing new or 
enhancing 
existing 
controls. 
(e.g., 
introduction of a new product, or service, a 
merger or an acquisition, opening in a new 
location, new correspondent arrangements) 
 
 Not updating the risk assessment annually or 
on ad-hoc basis (ad hoc review might be 
triggered by events such as   introduction of 
new products, services, technologies, merger 
or acquisition, expansion of the business (e.g., 
new locations)).  
 
 Undertaking risk assessment of the new 
products & services without taking into 
account the related inherent risk and 
controls derived from leading industry 
practices, guidelines/typologies from FATF 
and the Wolfsberg group.

1.3 -  Implementation of AML/CFT Risk Based Approach 
Examples of compliant / good practice 
Examples of non-compliance / poor practice 
 Clear criteria are established for client 
risk assessments/rating. This includes 
client business and occupation risk 
factors, beneficial ownership, source 
of funds/wealth, products, services 
and transactions, delivery channels 
and geographical risks.  
 
 Some customers’ types classified 
automatically high risk and subject to 
EDD regardless of other factors as a 
result of risk assessment: customers 
from countries that are subject to 
international sanctions, FATF listed 
jurisdictions, PEPs, etc.  
 
 The scope of CDD and monitoring 
scenarios are being determined based 
on client’s risk profile.  
 The client risk profile does not incorporate all 
of the following risk factors: customer risk, 
product & service risk, delivery channel risk 
and geographic risk, transaction patterns.  
 
 Customer risk profile and risk rating is  not 
being revised/changed on the basis of 
change in customer behavior, conduct of 
transactions not matching the customers 
profile and transactions to/from high risk 
countries, etc.   
 
 Different client’s risk ratings maintained in 
several systems (e.g., Core Remittance 
System and AML/CFT System);  as a result,  
client’s EDD information was not fully 
available and some clients were not 
subjected to enhanced monitoring.

 Clear processes are established to 
gather information from the client on 
purpose and nature of business 
relationship and to verify it.  
 
 Frequency and content (scope) of 
CDD review is informed by customer 
risk score, e.g., high-risk clients CDD 
information is being reviewed at least 
annually.  
 
 Frequency of the review is being 
determined based on customer risk 
profile (risk rating) and approved list

 Onboarding of corporate customers is 
handled at Centralized hub and 
subject to Compliance approval.   
 
 PEPs-related 
risk 
management 
system includes (1) PEP identification

reliable 
public

(2)

business 
relationship

transactions, (4) verification checks on

(5) annual review of PEP profiles (CDD 
and transactions data). 
 
 Transactions 
to/from 
high 
risk 
countries and clients  from high risk 
countries are subject to enhanced 
monitoring and other EDD measures. 
 
 
 
 Customers were not risk rated, e.g., 
Corporate and retail customers.  
 
 First line of defense (e.g., customer facing 
staff in branches/locations) does not have a 
possibility to see customer risk rating; as a 
result, this might have a negative impact on 
effectiveness of monitoring of high-risk 
transactions 
or 
activities 
(especially 
concerning clients who are subject to EDD 
measures).   
 
 High risk clients such as PEPs, customers 
transacting 
digitally, 
cash 
intensive 
customers, customers engaged in high risk 
businesses, etc. were not properly rated i.e., 
risks emanating from these customers were 
not properly understood and, as a result, 
weaker mitigating measures have been

 Country risks are not properly assessed and 
had been subject to override without proper 
approvals and mitigates. 
 
 Not having procedures in place to identify 
and verify if a client and beneficial owner of 
a legal entity is a PEP, family member or

 Lack of proper measures to handle the 
AML/CFT 
risk 
efficiently 
and 
adopt 
wholesale cutting loose of entire classes of 
customer 
relationships 
(wholesale 
de-
risking) without application of risk mitigation

from 
high

countries, 
charitable institutions / NPOs etc.

and after careful investigation of the matter it was established (evidenced) that the client in fact is not a 
person/entity subject to international financial sanctions. 
Black list in this context means a list of the customers, e.g., (1) with whom the licensee has terminated business

1.5 -  Ongoing monitoring and identification of suspicious activity 
Examples of compliant / good practice 
Examples of non-compliance / poor practice 
 
 All existing customers are screened on 
an ongoing basis (at least periodically) 
to identify any new designations. All 
payments screened against sanctions 
lists at the time of execution of each 
transaction.  
 
 Sanction screening includes financial 
institution employees, consultant and 
third party such as vendors. 
 
 All wire transfers to and from high-risk 
countries are subject to enhanced 
monitoring (i.e., transactions are 
being thoroughly analyzed) by the 
compliance department. 
 
 Monitoring scenarios are adapted 
according to the risk group of a 
customer and risk level of products 
and services.  
 
 Enhanced monitoring scenarios are 
established for high-risk cases, i.e., 
high risk clients, products, payment 
means, geographical locations and 
transactions.  
 
 Separate scenarios exist to detect 
financing of terrorism as distinct from 
money laundering.  
 
 The analysis of potentially suspicious 
transactions is comprehensive, well 
documented and conclusions are fully 
justified.  
 
 
 
 
 Scenarios are not classified according to a 
risk-based approach to enable enhanced 
degree and nature of monitoring in case of 
high-risk situations. 
 
 Scenarios with regard to transactions 
undertaken by PEPs (individuals and BOs), 
transactions with high-risk countries and 
transactions relating to virtual assets are not 
built-in into the system.  
 
 AML/CFT System is not fine-tuned to avoid 
generation of a large number of false 
positive alerts. 
 
 Using outdated sanction screening lists. 
 
 Major shareholders/board members/senior 
management of the customers and the 
correspondent banks are not screened 
against the sanction lists at the time of on-

 Not resolving the sanction screening alerts

 No mechanism or scenarios developed to 
monitor 
customers’ 
transactions 
for 
investing/trading in the virtual currencies.  
 
 The analysis of alerts of corporate customer 
transactions i.e. conducting transactions to 
beneficiaries in different line of business or 
dealing in jurisdictions not warranted for its 
business.

Chapter 2: Risk based approach - On-boarding customers and 
correspondents. 
2.1 Customers 
The risk assessment of a customer requires MEE to allocate an appropriate risk rating to the 
customer. Risk ratings should be either descriptive, such as "low”, “medium” or "high" or a sliding 
ordinal numeric scale from 1 to 10, where 1 is lowest risk and 10 denotes highest risk. 
Depending on the outcome of the assessment of its customer's money laundering / terrorism 
financing risk, a MEE should decide to what degree CDD will need to be performed. For a 
customer exhibiting significant potential risk for money laundering / terrorism financing, the 
MEE is required to carry out Enhanced CDD. For customers rated as low risk, MEE shall carry out 
Simplified CDD. 
2.2 Correspondents 
The risk and vulnerability derived on the correspondent financial institutions is even more 
relevant when the transactions are handled through its correspondents or on behalf of business 
partners.   There is less control and influence that financial institutions can effectively exert over 
correspondent/business partners by virtue of them being third party organizations as opposed 
to company employees.  
Therefore, the financial institutions have to access the risk associated with correspondent / 
business partner to satisfy themselves that they comply with the identification and verification 
requirements as per the regulatory expectations. 
All correspondent bank / agent should be on boarded after undergoing a documented process 
of due diligence and risk assessment prior to activation. The risk assessment should cover the 
following aspects: 
i. 
Ownership and management structure 
ii. 
Its major business activities and customer base (Product risk and customer risk) 
iii. 
Its principal place of business and branch locations (Geographical risk) 
iv. 
Delivery / Distribution channel risk 
Documents such as shareholding structure, AML/CFT policies and identification documents for

Chapter 3: Transaction Monitoring 
 
3.1 
Transaction monitoring (“TM”) is a key control in MEEs anti-money laundering and 
countering the financing of terrorism (“AML/CFT”) policies and procedures:  
 After the risk assessment exercise during on-boarding customers, risks can also 
manifest later, over the course of customers’ business relations with the MEE. 
 The risk perceptions of the customer vary during the course of business and they 
can often be detected through the robust conduct of Transaction Monitoring 
 
3.2 An effective TM system enables MEEs to detect and assess whether customers’ transactions 
pose suspicion when considered against their respective backgrounds and profiles. TM 
systems also facilitate the holistic reviews of customer transactions over periods of time, in 
order to monitor for any unusual or suspicious trends, patterns or activities that may take 
place. 
 
3.3 TM involves a review of a customer’s activity to determine whether the nature and volume 
of such activity is consistent with information regarding the purpose of the business 
relationship and expected activity with the financial institution. 
 
3.4 In certain scenarios, TM occurs in the post-transaction phase to identify if the customers 
activity is in line with anticipated activity for that customer. 
 
Parameter and Scenario Setting 
3.5 When appropriately configured and implemented, TM parameters and thresholds enable 
MEEs to flag unusual transactions with a reasonable degree of certainty of potential ML/TF 
characteristics warranting further inquiry. MEEs should always ensure that their parameters 
and thresholds take into account their specific risks and context. 
3.6 Various scenarios to detect (Red flags).  
 Same sender sending to many different beneficiaries. 
 Many different senders sending to the same beneficiary. 
 Misrepresentation of recorded beneficiaries – same account number but different 
named individuals. 
 Aggregated frequent and small transactions. 

 
 
 
21 
 
 Transactions destined to reach unrelated parties or transactions with no clear 
economic purpose. 
 Compare anticipated volumes, value, frequency and transaction size. 
 Significant deviations from past account activity (or inactivity). 
 Non-justifiable source of funds used for transactions. 
 Inconsistent purpose of payments. 
 Destination of funds to high-risk jurisdictions/secrecy heavens. 
 Transactions carried out by nationals of High-Risk countries. 
 Transnational transactions, where a national of one country is remitting to another 
country with which he/she does not have any relation. 
 High percentage of transactions involving cash pick up. 
 Transactions where the purpose is a charitable donation. 
 An increase in international wire transfer activity to jurisdictions with no history of 
such activity or where the stated business of the customer does not warrant it. 
 Customer receives many small incoming wire transfers and then orders a large 
outgoing wire transfer to another country. 
 Customer make transfer just below threshold. 
 Customer over justifies or explains the transaction. 
 Customer is involved in transactions that are suspicious in nature, but pretend blind 
being involved in money laundering activities. 
 Customer appears to be acting on behalf of third party. 
 Customer provides false information or information you believe is unreliable. 
 You are aware or you become aware, from reliable sources that the customer is 
suspected to be involved in illegal activities. 
 Any other seemingly unexplainable situation or transaction volume that goes against 
normal business practices of customer. 
 Transaction seem inconsistent with the customer’s apparent financial standing or 
usual pattern of activities. 
 Customer trying to change large small value denomination into large value. 
 Company accounts whose transactions are solely conducted in cash without specific 
reason.  
 Customer seems unconcerned with exchange rates, cost associated with transfer. 
 Two customers coming together, but sending money to the same beneficiary or 
receiving funds from the same remitter. 
 Customer concealing the beneficial owners or having least knowledge about the 
beneficiary. 
 Two or more customers using the same customer ID / Contact numbers for 
remittances. 
 Customer refuses to disclose the source of cash / funds for undertaking transaction. 

 
 
 
22 
 
 Customer on frequent basis sends money to countries or regions, which are known 
for internet frauds. 
 Customer only seems to know the beneficiary details after reaching the exchange 
company. 
 Recurring wire transfers to virtual currency exchanges. 
 
3.7 MEEs should be mindful that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to configuring their TM 
rules, and that it is critical to ensure these are developed and calibrated in view of the risks 
they face, such as from their customer types, range of products, types of business activities, 
geographical exposures, cross-border nature and so forth.

Chapter 4: Other general guidelines 
4.1 
All licensees shall mandatorily register themselves with National Centre for Financial 
Information (NCFI) for dissemination of information. 
 
4.2 
Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) shall be filed within 30 days of detection of 
suspicious transaction by the financial institution. It is prohibited to communicate to any 
person involved in the transaction that the suspicious transaction report has been filed. 
A STR and/or the information contained in the STR must only be provided to NCFI or an 
appropriate law enforcement or supervisory authority when requested. 
 
4.3 
MEEs accepting cash directly into their bank account can pose a significant risk of money 
laundering. Criminals and associates prefer direct deposits, it makes them anonymous 
and allows multiple/unrelated parties to deposit illicit/unaccounted cash on behalf of one 
customer. MEEs shall implement measures to ensure that the cash deposited in their 
account has stemmed from the customer themselves or their authorized 
representatives. 
 
4.4 
Staff of financial institutions should be encouraged to report their suspicions, 
irrespective of the amount of triggers; where there is reasonable grounds to suspect that 
the funds are proceeds of criminal activity. 
 
4.5 
Originator information should be mandatorily collected for inward transfers. 
 
4.6 
MEEs shall display their list of branch locations in the company’s website. 
 
4.7 
Customers who should be restricted to use the business of Money Exchange 
Establishments 
 Customers involved in the business of illegal product or services. 
 Customers involved in unregulated or unauthorized financial / payment services / 
illegal remittance business. 
 Customers involved in drug related activities 
 Customers under the sanctions of the UN, the EU, the US, the UK and other 
national sanctions regimes 
 Shell banks and unlicensed financial / payment institutions. 
 Customers with known or suspected involvement in money laundering, terrorist 
financing, weapon of mass destruction proliferation, tax evasion or other 
financial crimes. 
 Anonymous accounts or accounts in fictitious name. 
 Multi-level marketing, pyramid schemes, referral marketing. 
 
Unregistered charities or NPOs and any anonymous payment mechanisms such 
as virtual/crypto-currencies, crowd funding etc.
